subsubtopic: PROPOSED UNILATERAL DECLARATION OF MANAGEMENT OF MARINE RESOURCES TO EDGE OF CONTINENTAL SHELF-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I rise to ask leave of the House to present a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
Having regard to the fact that the fishing industry of this country is in danger of being totally destroyed as a result of overfishing off our coast by foreign fishing fleets; and, in light of the failure of the Geneva Law of the Sea Conference and all other such conferences dating back to 1959 to agree on a solution to the problem, I move, seconded by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse):
That this government establish a date within the present year, 1975, on which this country will, in the absence of a satisfactory agreement by the other fishing nations of the world to reduce their fishing efforts over our continental shelf, unilaterally assert its control over the marine resources to the edge of the continental shelf and the slopes thereto, thereby enabling Canada to properly manage, harvest and rehabilitate our fishery resources and, further, that this country's delegates to the forthcoming ICNAF meetings be instructed to convey this ultimatum to all other member nations at the June 6 meeting of that body.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIEW OF INADEQUATE ESCALATION OF PENSIONS OF RETIRED EMPLOYEES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to present a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It arises from yesterday's announcement concerning the escalation of the pensions of Canadian National retired employees. It is a motion which I hope the House will see fit to accept.
Sir, in December several deputy ministers retired on sizeable pensions and received cost of living increases of more than 10 per cent in January, the very next month. Canadian National proposes to escalate the pensions of those who retired more than two years ago by a formula involving increases from 6 per cent down; for those who retired in 1973 and 1974 there is to be no escalation at all. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That this House hereby declares that the recently announced minimal cost of living increases in Canadian National pensions in the case of those who retired prior to January 1, 1973, and the refusal of the CNR to grant any cost of living increases at all in the case of those who retired in 1973 and in 1974, are totally unacceptable, and this House calls on the Canadian National Railways to review this matter forthwith, it being the view of this House that all pensions should be escalated at least by the percentage of the rise in the cost of living.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to bring forward an extremely urgent motion requiring immediate attention.
Given the fact that the revelations heard before the Quebec organized crime inquiry have shown unquestionably that Canadians, and particularly Quebecers, have eaten tainted meat sold by unscrupulous individuals, and that the repressive measures provided in the statutes are far too weak to dissuade tainted meat dealers from poisoning the population, since the fines are under $100, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That this House consider the measures to be taken in order that the tainted meat dealers upon conviction for a first office, be liable to imprisonment for a term of at least two years without any respite nor parole and, for a second offence, to imprisonment for a term of five years without any respite nor parole, in order to protect Canadian citizens from the disgusting doings of those who sell tainted meat for human consumption.

Mr. Chairman, with unemployment holding at well above 7 per cent of the work force, and giving clear indications of rising considerably above that figure as the year goes on, it is the responsibility of those of us who sit in parliament to examine the causes of the economic stagnation we are experiencing, and make positive suggestions for correcting it.
The basic reason for the slowing down of the economy has been the steady decrease in the volume of exports and the increase in the volume of imports that have been taking place during the past 18 months. The prices of our products have steadily become less competitive with those quoted by other countries, and the quality and design of our products have not been good enough to overcome this disadvantage.
During the month of April this deteriorating situation was temporarily halted by the erosion of the value of the Canadian dollar, which has, during this short period, made our exports more attractive in price, and imports from other countries less attractive in the Canadian market. However, this temporary help cannot be counted on to last for very long, and the dollar has already risen well above the level to which it dropped a couple of weeks ago. Therefore we must look for other remedies to correct our sick economy, and I suggest we examine three main approaches: first, increasing productivity; second, increasing industrial research and development; and third, lowering unit labour costs.
Taking a look at productivity we find that during the 28 years since 1947, when the government first started to measure it on an annual basis, industrial productivity in Canada has increased at an average annual rate of 3.2 per cent a year. Examining our performance since 1970, we find that in 1971 productivity increased by 3 per cent over 1970, or slightly below the average rate; in 1972 the increase was reduced to 2.6 per cent, in 1973 to 1.5 per cent, and in 1974 there was an actual loss of one half of one per cent. The present indication is that the slide will continue at about the same pace during the present year.
What can be done to increase productivity and thereby help make our products more competitive? To do so we must offer incentives which will persuade producers that they will be able to pay for the new plant, machinery, and production systems they will have to buy, in a reasonably short space of time, and in this way make it as easy as possible for them to meet the high expenditures usually

May 28, 1975

involved. The kind of incentive I have in mind would be one whereby (1) all capital expenditures may be written off in the period decided upon by the plant owner; (2) a plant would be rewarded in the form of a generous cash bonus at the end of the year in proportion to its increase in productivity during the year, compared to the base year- the last full year before the plan goes into operation.
This form of incentive has been very effective in increasing productivity in such countries as Japan and West Germany where spectacular results have been achieved since the end of the second world war. There is no reason why such an incentive would be any less successful in this country.
In addition to price, we know very well that quality and design are also very important in making our products competitive. It is obvious that we must spend at least as high a proportion of our GNP on research and development as our chief competitors do, if we are to hold our own in this important field. To see how we have been doing in this regard as compared to our major industrial competitors, we should look at the latest figures published by the OECD. These show what percentage of its GNP each of these countries spends on research and development. The figures are as follows: United States 2.8 per cent; United Kingdom 2.4 per cent; France 1.9 per cent; West Germany 1.7 per cent; Japan 1.5 per cent; Canada 1.3 per cent. It is obvious that we have been doing badly in comparison to our major competitors in this regard.
To capture new markets which are looking for new and better designed products, and to reduce costs and become more competitive, it is obvious that we must carry out a great deal more research and development in this country. To bring this about we should allow industry to write off 200 per cent of the cost of current and capital expenditures on research and development in excess of those made in the base year-the last full year before the program is introduced. In addition to writing off the full cost in one year, it will put a considerable cash reward in the pocket of a company undertaking the research.
The kind of program I have outlined has been successful in significantly increasing the volume of industrial research in countries where it has been introduced, and will prove equally effective in Canada.
Finally, what can we do, in addition to increasing productivity, to reduce the labour cost of the products we must sell? There is a great deal of business which Canadian companies are unable to compete for because of low labour costs in the foreign countries where the products are made. If Canadian companies are to be able to compete for a good proportion of this business, and thereby obtain additional employment for Canadians, they must have an incentive which will enable them to reduce their labour costs on this potential new business to a level where they are within striking distance of these low foreign rates. Then, by accepting a lower than normal margin of profit on this extra business in order to get started, they can compete for these orders and stand a good chance of obtaining a reasonable proportion of them. What kind of incentive will do the job?
The government should say to all business-not just manufacturers and processors-that it will reward overall
Business of Supply
increases in employment during the year by way of an employment incentive which will be paid in direct proportion to the increases that are made. It is simply a matter of comparing the total number of man-years of employment by a company in the tax year under consideration with the last full year before the plan is put into operation-which will be the base year. The employment incentive would be paid in proportion to the increase in employment and the general wage level of the plant concerned, and the company will thus be able to calculate well in advance just what amounts of money it would receive for various increases in employment. This will enable Canadian businessmen to calculate in advance how much their labour costs would be reduced on additional business which the employment incentive would make it possible for them to go after. All such business obtained in this way will be a net gain for Canadian employment.
The three incentives which I have outlined will pay for themselves many times over in the years ahead, in the following ways: (1) We can drastically cut the present far too high expenditure on unemployment insurance by stimulating the economy and enabling people to find work. The potential in this regard is at least $1.5 billion of the $3 billion a year which we are at present paying out in unemployment insurance payments. (2) We can greatly increase tax revenues, because (a) more people will be working and paying income taxes; (b) more commodities will be sold, and will be paying additional commodity taxes, and (c) the increased volume of business will lower unit costs of production, and make available more profits to tax.
I think it is obvious that the government has shown great negligence in allowing our export trade to deteriorate seriously during the past 18 months without introducing the measures which were available to it for re-establishing the competitiveness of our products. It is equally obvious that the minister must take the primary responsibility for this sorry state of affairs, and has in no way justified the salary he is being paid as a minister.
I therefore move:
That Vote 1 of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce be reduced from $67,157,000 to $67,137,000.

Mr. Chairman, I do not accept at all the principle that the 15 minutes can be transferred to govern-

ment or other members. Nobody in this House has the authority to transfer time accruing to each member, and I do not accept at all that procedure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In any case, the hon. member for Lon-gueuil was also present when the agreement was reached, and it was unanimously agreed that each member would be entitled to 15 minutes to use as he wishes, either to make a speech or put questions to the minister. Then, the minister may be recognized at any time, if he wishes to use his 15 minutes-he is in his right-whether he uses his time at the end of the debate is his decision.

Mr. Chairman, I am prepared to grant the minister the indulgence he wants so as to give him the opportunity of speaking, providing it is understood that he replies to the questions I am going to raise rather than to those of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings.
I would tend to support the motion moved by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings if it were made retroactive, because I think that just about every minister of industry, trade and commerce that we have had in this country has been derelict in his duty. I do not know whether this is the fault of the minister we have had at any particular time or whether it is because of the advice the minister gets from his departmental officials, but I rather suspect that it is because of the advice he gets from his department. In any event, it is not our job to question that or know about it. After all, it is the minister who is held responsible in this House.
Wherever ministers have been getting their advice on economic and industrial policy in Canada it has been terrible, and almost invariably policy has been based on continentalism all the way through. Whenever we talk about productivity or the rationalization of industry, it is always rationalization with the United States.
The chickens are now coming home to roost. Up until recently, when the United States was fighting a war, there were tremendous demands by the United States for all kinds of products Americans could not produce themselves, so the problems in respect of foreign ownership and their consequence on our productivity were obscured. Now the United States is in a recession, and fortunately for humanity's sake the war is over. We are now beginning to see the consequences of foreign ownership in this country.
I should like to point to one industry, although I could point to many, to show that the effect of foreign ownership has not been a Machiavellian scheme to brainwash us or change our culture, but has been one of giving us an incredibly inefficient industrial structure. We see this everywhere we look; whether it is in respect of chemicals, rubber or electronics, the intrusion of foreign ownership in this country has prevented Canada from living up to its potential.
There seems to have been some kind of reverse alchemy at work which, in this country with all its advantages, natural resources, people and energy, has turned our gold into dust. They have reversed the process. We would have been better off without a Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce than having one that has led us into conti
Business of Supply
nentalism, whether in respect of the Canada-U.S. auto agreement or the rubber industry. We are now beginning to see what happens.
Most of us have received a petition from the Canadian rubber workers asking us to support increases in tariffs. This industry is in danger of going under. It is not as though the minister was not warned about the consequences of the situation. For years it has been pointed out that this kind of attitude on the part of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, with lack of coordination of regional development policy, foreign ownership legislation, and combines legislation, would lead to an incredibly inefficient rubber industry, almost totally foreign owned and inefficient compared to that of the United States.
The argument has always been that we have overcome this kind of inefficiency by low wage rates in Canada. Traditionally this is what we have done; we have overcome the inefficient structure of certain industries by paying our workers less than those in the United States. This cannot go on forever. The wages of our workers are now approaching those of workers in the United States, but our industrial productivity is not approaching that of the United States, and that is why the cry goes up that our workers are getting too much and are asking for too much. The fact is that they are not getting too much and they are not asking for more than their U.S. counterparts who are doing less work. But our industry is certainly not as effective as industry in the United States.
At the time we brought Michelin into Canada there was a warning that the rubber makers in this country would ask for tariff concessions. They got those tariff concessions to rationalize continentalism. The result is that production is being shifted to the United States. That is the consequence of branch plant economies. The minute problems develop in one country where the corporation originates the branch plant, that part of the world suffers, and we are paying the price of being a branch plant economy with this production shift to the United States. In spite of every give-away the Minister of Finance has been able to put forward, including concessions in the way of corporate taxes and write-offs to offset the DISC program in the United States, this production is being shifted out of the country.
There are many things that could be said and that I would like to say, but 15 minutes is not enough time in which to vent my anger about the insane policies pursued by the government. I do not think 15 minutes will be enough time for the minister to reply or to explain away generations of incompetence in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in directing industrial forces in this country. He is not going to have 15 minutes, but whatever time he has will not be long enough to accomplish that.
Since the minister has asked us to pose specific questions, perhaps he will have the courtesy to listen to those I wish to ask. The minister has said on many occasions that there is no such thing as industrial strategy. He laughs at the idea of an over-all industrial strategy. Instead of that he says we have sectoral strategy-we have specific strategies for specific industries. In view of the enormous layoffs in the rubber industry and the demands by workers in that industry for some tariff protection, will the minister

tell the House today what is the strategy of his department regarding the rubber industry, and what he intends to do about providing jobs in that industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge is perfectly correct when he says I do not believe it is possible to devise and tailor a great big blueprint which might be called an industrial strategy for Canada. Indeed, I believe, as the government does, that the right way is to deal with each industry on a case by case basis. Each industry has particular requirements, particular constraints, particular opportunities, particular weaknesses and particular strengths.
In respect of the tire industry, my department has already entered into discussions with Canadian tire manufacturers, which the hon. member was quite accurate in describing as being largely if not completely foreign controlled. These companies have in the past seen their strategy in terms of North American strategy. What we are anxious to do is work with them to develop a rationalization and a more modern industry that will operate in terms of an optimum scale rather than with some rather small plants as at the present time.
The present situation is the result of a number of factors, partly related to the automobile industry itself. That is to say, the industry is suffering a very significant depression at the present time. The present situation is partly related to the fact that the Canadian tire manufacturers have not moved as rapidly as their parent companies toward radial tires. At the present time I think some 75 per cent of all tires going on new commercial or passenger vehicles are radial. There is not a capacity for radial tires here at the present time. I am told that a number of manufacturers have already started quite significant investment plans to modernize or convert their plants to radial tires.
The other reason for unemployment is that there is a heavy inventory of non-radial tires, which has to be seen in conjunction with the condition of the automobile industry at the present time. I would hope that by putting this particular industry on an industrialized and rational basis we will be able to work out with them a more efficient industry which will have a Canadian perspective rather than the kind of perspective it has had in the past, which is part of the North American strategy and has a "made in U.S." label on it.

I hope the minister realizes the damning nature of some of the things he has said. He has said that, given the recession which is taking place and the change in demand now for radial tires, the bulk of the investment and the first production has been in the United States while Canadians are being asked to work off the inventories of non-radial tires. We are supposed to take the brunt of this technological change. I suggest this is the result of branch plant economy. I am not suggesting it is unnatural for the United States to behave in this way. Their first interest is in the United States just as our first interest is in Canada. They are naturally going to look after their problems in the United States before they look after our problems in Canada.
I am encouraged to some extent by what the minister has said in that it would indicate he is at least aware of

the problem. Up until now there has been a tendency to laugh -and suggest that we are always talking about foreign ownership, blowing its consequences out of all proportion. There has been a tendency to say this has nothing to do with our problems, and that the best solution is to rationalize on the basis of continentalism. Apparently now there is at least some awareness of the situation.
How is the minister going to enforce on foreign corporations his suggested program for rationalization in Canada? What specifically is the minister proposing to these companies, and what kind of assurances and protections are being looked into in order to see that this kind of thing does not happen again where, when there is a problem, the United States looks after itself first, and then we are used as the overflow to catch up if there is any kind of a shortfall in their production?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think the first point which should be made is that nothing will happen in the industry unless the industry itself sees there is a problem; that is, unless the Canadian industry sees that it is losing out relative to the tire industry of other countries. That is the first point with which we must deal. The second point is that it must be in their interest to invest in Canada because there is no way I know that the government can force them to invest. Clearly it must be in their interest. They have to decide that the market is growing and that there is an opportunity for them.
I think the third point is to make them aware of the problems that are likely to be realized if the industry continues to have as many separate plants as it presently has. I think that with the degree of scale that is now required, for every tire manufactured we will probably require fewer rather than more tire manufacturing companies in Canada. I think very likely there may be incentive programs already within my department which could assist them in this rationalization. The fourth lever I would suggest to the hon. member is the moral suasion lever. I think sometimes this probably is underestimated. I think most of the individuals managing these companies in Canada want to see their industry developed in tune with Canada's needs.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is not a naive person. I do not accuse him of being one, but what he is saying is absolutely incredible. He is saying that the government is not directly interested in this matter beyond moral suasion, and will depend on the companies and on the instinct of this industry to do it.
I am not questioning the good instincts of businessmen or their desire to be good Canadians. I am sure that is true. What I am questioning is their ability. They are locked into an archaic system from which they cannot break out.
Unless the Canadian government is prepared to move in and do something, then nothing will be done. How do you expect people who are competing with each other internationally in the rubber and tire industry, suddently to get together in Canada and work out a system which is in the national interest? Surely this is a time when, much as we may be concerned about the particular interest of a company, we must be far more concerned about the national
May 28, 1975

interest, and the only one who is in a position to determine that, and act on behalf of the people and make it stick, is the minister himself, and not some well intentioned president of a rubber company.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I can only take it that the hon. member is suggesting that the Canadian government nationalize this industry-
I just say "do something".

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: -that it acquire all the existing companies, nationalize them, and then tell its own industry where it should go. This is not the philosophy or approach of this government. Our approach is to work with private industry and show it that it is in its interest that what it does will be in the national interest, and therefore it will be in our interest. I think we have been successful in this and in other areas in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, since the minister seems to be in such high spirits this afternoon, I should like to give him the opportunity to show his mettle and ask him a few questions dealing with the textile and clothing as well as the furniture industry.
As the minister knows, both are major industries in our country, and especially in eastern Canada. The companies involved employ a large number of workers and they are faced with problems because of foreign competition. It is basically not a matter of dumping, but a matter of competition which companies find extremely difficult to face.
Moreover, if you talk with union leaders not of strike but of production, of satisfaction with working conditions, of the future of that industry, they will complain that they have no say when discussions are held. When I meet with the owners of furniture or textile plants, and there are several in my riding, they complain of not knowing exactly what is the overall policy of Canada with respect to textile or furniture.
On the other hand, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as I told the minister in the House this week, sent a letter recently to a mayor from the St. Maurice Valley stating that the federal government was about to introduce an overall textile and clothing policy for Canada. To complete my question, the minister is aware of imports of some polyester and cotton fibres and other kinds of fibres from the Republics of Korea and Taiwan and a number of other countries, and the Textile Board was ordered to inquire into those imports. The results of those inquiries are in fact strictly provisional, but then again are not meant to pave the way for only an employment protection policy which has already been implemented in Canada, but also an overall policy designed to give the economy of those industries a new impetus.
I would therefore like the minister to tell me first of all if his department now has the required data to implement an overall policy on textile as well as clothing and furniture. Is his department aware of the situation in those plants? Is it aware of the fact that almost 50 per cent of the Quebec market is under the control of foreign markets in those areas of industry and trade. Finally, I ask the minister when he intends to announce an overall policy in this
Business of Supply
respect. As I said at the outset, those industries are the backbone of our economy, especially our Quebec economy. If they were to disappear, I believe we would have two or three times the current unemployment rate.
I am very much concerned about the future of these industries, remembering what happened with the shoemaking industry. The government acted there, but when that industry had disappeared. Therefore, my question is quite clear. Although it deals with complex and elaborate problems, I would give the minister the time to bring forward am answer hopefully encouraging not only to the owners of these industries, but also to the workers who, although intent on staying on the job, are extremely concerned about the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a great deal of work was done by my predecessor in respect of the textile policy for Canada. That work was done with the representatives of the unions and with the representatives of the companies in the textile industry. It took place over a period of probably two years. The background to that policy at that time was the fact that there was a real threat from the low wage countries of the world.
The textile industry, if we go back to about 1970 when the present textile policy had its beginning, was an industry which was characterized with all the typical features of a declining industry. Employment had been going down, wages were very low, and imports were increasing as a percentage of the domestic market. Many of the plants were rather old fashioned, many had not received any new equipment because of the declining situation. In many cases, managements were out of touch. They had not introduced new measures. Very little had been done with respect to design and fashion, and no real effort had been made to look at the export markets of the world because of the considerable defensive position of the industry toward imports.
The textile policy was announced in 1970 with the legislation which provided for the Textile and Clothing Board. The basic elements of the textile policy, which is now in place, are to provide an incentive to companies to modernize and make themselves internationally competitive. The instrument for that was the Textile and Clothing Board. The employers and producers have the option of going to the board and seeking support for various kinds of restraints which would be negotiated with the low cost countries-voluntary quotas, if you like-and the assistance of the Export and Import Permits Act supports this policy.
A considerable amount of investment took place as a result of that policy, and for the first time employment started to rise, not decline, and wage levels came up a little. I will not argue that wage levels in this industry approach the national average in manufacturing; I think they are still significantly lower, but they improved and the outlook improved.
Various other steps were taken to assist those who might be laid off as a result of the rationalization of

May 28, 1975
Business of Supply
smaller units into larger units. The background to all that was the low cost import.
Today the situation is quite different. It is still a situation where the low cost import can provide a considerable downward pressure on the Canadian market in terms of price, to some extent in terms of pre-empting part of the Canadian market, but it is not nearly the problem it was, relatively speaking, back in the early 1970's.
The real problem today is that industrial activity in the textile industry in Canada is down because the market is down. It is down because the distributing trades, the retailers and wholesalers, have been cutting their inventories, and so they have not been placing their orders with their regular Canadian suppliers. That situation has been aggravated by imports from abroad, not just from the low cost countries but as well from the industrial countries, such as the United States. That is a significant change in the situation.
We have introduced a large number of measures. We have put many of these products, in fact most, on the import control list to ensure that we have precise and up to date information on imports wherever those imports may come from. I have had a number of discussions with the industry's representatives, both labour and management, with respect to the state of their industry and their outlook for it. We have negotiated restraints, voluntary quotas if you like, with the countries of origin of many of these products.
So far as the textile industry is concerned, the situation in the short term at present reflects market conditions in the world and in Canada. I think the long term outlook for the industry is still strong and I expect the industry to pick up and to continue to grow. Indeed a number of textile manufacturers are making significant investments to the tune of $40 million and $50 million.

Mr. Chairman, before my time is expired, I would like to tell the minister about one disappointment. I hope it will not be ignored, but will produce positive results. One of the departments where communications and information are most important, as far as business is concerned, is Industry, Trade and Commerce. It has a particularly high number of complex branches and programs. Industry owners I know in Victoriaville, Prince-ville, Daveluyville, Warwick, Sainte-Croix are unanimous.
In other parts of Quebec also, I hear the same questions. Everytime I speak with those people, I am asked whether Industry, Trade and Commerce would not do such and such a thing, whether it could not help them know foreign markets so they can export. Can they be told what products are made in other countries?
Of course, this extremely important and worthwhile information comes from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I believe, Mr. Chairman, and I submit very humbly and very respectfully to the minister that there is certainly a gap in the information on the various programs available. This valuable and essential information which our constituent and especially the owners of these plants, need to develop their business has to be made available in our constituencies.

Mr. Chairman, I would like the minister to tell me whether he his aware of this root problem? I know that his departmental officials have this information, but if we put ouselves in the shoes of the businessman who can hardly manage to run his business, we find that he does not have the time to learn all about these various programs which are sometimes good and sometimes not so good, but which are always extremely important.
I am also well aware that by writing to the minister, we can obtain material such as the hon. member is now showing to me, but sending this material to the constituents involved does not necessarily solve the problem.
I should like to know not only what efforts the minister intends to make to publish information on those various programs, since this material already exists, but whether he intends to increase his staff or to improve his communication system so that the businessman may obtain everything he needs either to diversify his products or to promote the export of his production to other countries or to improve his own production in his own plant? I believe, Mr. Chairman, that I represent a highly industrialized constituency and that all my constituents have some grievances have some grievances or requests to make in this connection.
My question is very simple: Is the minister aware of this problem? Does he want the people to benefit as much as possible from the various programs of his department, and what efforts does he intend to make in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, we certainly do. I agree with the hon. member when he says that it is sometimes difficult to sort out which particular program might be of assistance to a manufacturer or exporter.
We have a large variety of programs. For example, on the design side we have the Industrial Design Assistance Program on a cost sharing basis which assists, for example, furniture manufacturers to build or design new units. We have Fashion Canada which helps textile manufacturers on the design side. We have the GAAB Board which helps industries to restructure themselves. We have the Productivity Improvement Program, again on a cost sharing basis, which is aimed at assisting the management of these firms to improve their productivity and to make them more competitive. We have a program for the export market development which is aimed at assisting the selfstarter manufacturer to find new markets abroad. Again it is on a 50-50 cost sharing basis. I would be very pleased to provide the hon. member with this information. Perhaps that would be the easiest way of satisfying him on this point.

I think that the minister has not fully grasped my question. I am well aware of these different programs. However, I am not in a position to inform each and everyone of these industrialists, because I am not an expert in each of the fields concerned. What I am asking the minister, is what means he uses to ensure that such information be truly and well used by the industrialists. Can the minister dispatch a few of his officials to visit on location one of these furniture manufacturing plants, either Victoriaville Furniture, or Fonderie Sainte-Croix,
May 28, 1975

which is one of the most important Canadian foundries and which is precisely in need of advice to diversify its production, in Canada as well as abroad?
Has the minister such services at his disposal to vulgarize and explain to the common folk the multitude of documents with which I am well acquainted? But not being an industrialist, I cannot explain all the aspects of each of these programs to the industrialists in my constituency. Can the minister, within his own department, intensify or even increase the number of experts to visit industrialists and encourage them not only to expand but also diversify and improve their production?

Mr. Chairman, in my remarks pertaining to the estimates of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and as the minister has to leave temporarily on important business, I should like to review the responsibilities of this department with particular reference to the federal government and export trade.
The Canadian economy continues to be vitally dependent on international trade. Canadian exports of goods and services now account for about 25 per cent of gross national expenditure at market prices. The share of export trade in total national income has increased steadily since 1959 when it represented about 18 per cent of all goods and services produced in Canada. The Canadian economy, therefore, is becoming increasingly dependent, and therefore vulnerable, to fluctuations in external demand.
With the current economic slowdown in most major industrialized countries, international competition is intense, and increased exports are not easily achieved. A successful Canadian export trade can be assured by combining good products, efficient production, and aggressive, intelligent marketing, with government support.
Federal government support is provided mainly through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Export Development Corporation. ITC assists Canadian industry from research, design and development through the production and marketing of the finished product. The EDC provides insurance, guarantees, loans and other financial facilities to assist Canadian exporters. The EDC is a Crown agency which reports to parliament through the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
In addition to ITC and EDC, there are numerous other federal government organizations that are involved in Canadian export trade. Many of these other organizations are responsible to different ministries, and I want to make reference to this again before I close.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was established in 1969 as a result of the merger of the departments of trade and commerce and of industry. The department has the responsibility for stimulating the establishment, growth and efficiency of the manufacturing, processing and tourist industries in Canada and the de-
Business of Supply
velopment of export trade and external trade policies. With respect to export trade specifically, responsibility lies with the senior assistant deputy minister of international trade.
Under the ADM of international are the ADM Export Development, Trade Commissioner Services, and the ADM International Trade Relations. Departmental units involved in international trade within ITC are the office of general relations, office of special import policy, export and import permits branch, the international bureaux, trade commissioner service, office of international special projects, financing and aid branch, grain marketing office, transportation services branch, fairs and missions branch, and the program office (export market development) which handles the administration of the program for export market development.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce's functions include: improving access of Canadian goods and services into external markets through trade negotiations; contributing to the improvement of world trading conditions; providing support services for industrial and trade development, including information, import analysis and tariff services; analysing the implications for Canadian industry, trade and commerce and for tourism of government policies related thereto in order to contribute to the formulation and review of those policies; and compiling and updating detailed information on trends and developments in Canada and abroad related to the manufacturing and processing and tourist industries.
The department operates eight regional offices located across Canada, and the trade commissioner service which has 82 trade offices in 57 countries. The minister also reports to parliament on behalf of Statistics Canada and the Export Development Corporation.
Boards and other organizations reporting to the minister are the General Adjustment Assistance Board, the Machinery and Equipment Advisory Board, the Pharmaceutical Industry Development Advisory Committee, the National Design Council, the Standards Council of Canada, the Textile and Clothing Board, the Preparatory Commission for Metric Conversion, and the minister's advisory council.
The Export Development Corporation, a Crown corporation, reports to parliament through the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and is empowered by federal statute to encourage, facilitate, and develop Canadian export trade by providing credit insurance, guarantees, loans and other financial assistance to enable Canadian exporters to meet international competition. The EDC, which succeeded the Export Credits Insurance Corporation in 1969, has its head office in Ottawa and district offices in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. Direction of the affairs of the corporation is vested in a 12 member board.
The main functions of EDC are to insure the Canadian exporter against non-payment due to credit or political risks beyond the control of either the exporter or the buyer when export sales are made on normal credit terms. Almost all export transactions are insurable, not only those involving goods or technical services but also those involving invisible exports such as managerial services, advertising programs, the licensing or sale of patents,

trademarks, copyrights, etc. Its functions are also to issue appropriate guarantees to chartered banks or to any person providing non-recourse supplier financing in respect of an export sale. Guarantees may also be issued in connection with a loan made to a foreign buyer for the pruchase of Canadian goods and services.
It also finances foreign buyers of Canadian capital goods and related services when extended credit terms are necessary and are not available from commercial lenders. Major engineering and other technical services-but not feasibility studies-may be financed, even when such sales are not related to the export of goods. It also has a function to insure Canadian investments abroad against non-commercial risks such as loss through confiscation, expropriation, war or revolution, or the inability to repatriate capital or earnings.
The General Adjustment Assistance Board administers the general adjustment assistance program. The program helps manufacturers take advantage of export opportunities arising from the Kennedy Round; assists manufacturers of textiles, clothing goods or footwear to improve their competitive position in domestic or export markets; and aids those who have been injured, or threatened with injury, as a result of Kennedy Round reductions of Canadian tariffs. Financial assistance is also made available in the form of government insurance on loans, direct loans and grants to manufacturers for restructuring projects necessitated by tariff changes. The board has members representing both private industry and government, and reports to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.

The objectives of the Standards Council of Canada are to foster and promote voluntary standardization in fields relating to the construction, manufacture, production, quality, performance and safety of buildings, structures, manufactured articles and products and other goods, including components thereof, not expressely provided for by law, as a means of advancing the national economy, benefiting the health, safety and welfare of the public, assisting and protecting consumers, facilitating domestic and international trade and furthering international co-operation in the field of standards.
A comprehensive statistical service on Canada's external trade is available from Statistics Canada, formerly the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. In addition to broad quantitative data published in monthly, quarterly, and annual reports covering import and export trade by commodities and countries, Statistics Canada offers a service of special tabulations of unpublished data in a variety of combinations to meet almost any specific need for export or import figures. The administrative head of the bureau is the Chief Statistician of Canada, who has the rank of a deputy head of a department and reports to parliament through the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Other federal government organizations and related agencies with involvement in Canadian export trade include the Agricultural Products Board, the Bank of

Canada, Canadian Development Corporation, Canadian Grain Commission, Canadian International Development Agency, Canadian International Development Board, Canadian Transport Commission, Canadian Wheat Board, Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, Department of Communications, Department of External Affairs, Department of Finance, Department of National Revenue, Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, National Energy Board and National Farm Products Marketing Council.
In addition to the foregoing, other federal government organizations and related agencies with indirect or peripheral involvement in Canadian export trade include Air Canada, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Canadian Film Development Corporation, Canadian Government Specifications Board, Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, Canadian Patents and Development Ltd., Defence Construction Ltd., Industrial Development Bank, Inter-American Development Bank (Canadian Section), International Development Research Centre, Machinery and Equipment Advisory Board, Ministry of State for Science and Technology, (Bilateral Co-operation Division), National Design Council, Post Office Department, Preparatory Commission for Metric Conversion, Metric Commission, Tariff Board, Telesat Canada, Textile and Clothing Board, Uranium Canada Ltd., and the Interdepartmental Committee on External Relations.

I bet you turned him down.

This shocked me. That people are panhandling openly in front of the Bank of Canada may be a sign of the times.
Like many Canadians, I am deeply disappointed with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I am disappointed at his lack of energy, imagination, and leadership in the many fields of trade and industry. His efforts could be best described as a holding action-holding on for dear life, holding on and hoping for some economic miracle that will reverse the dangerous course we are now travelling.
We are paying today for the patched up programs, the ill-conceived plans and decisions taken in the past few years. We are paying the price for poorly thought out programs which were put into effect with much fanfare and publicity. The minister gives the impression that he is dealing only with shadows; he never seems to come to grips with the substance. The minister has a standard, stock answer to any question regarding industrial initiatives: "My officials are studying the matter." This usually leads to the hiring of a private consultant who recommends the establishment of yet another alphabet program under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Then again if you ask the minister a question about industry or trade, he reels off programs called PAIT, DIP, FLIP, FLOP or SLUSH, or other programs which have been put in place. I do not intend to make light of these programs-SLUSH is the name that amuses me. Many of these programs existed for many years, and they still exist. Many of them are ineffective, or not properly oriented. At best they are marshmallow programs. They have all the impact and impression on our industry of a marshmallow. We need industry programs which go further than the handing out of grants. All that program directors do consistently is publish a multi-coloured booklet.
Business of Supply
I submit that what we really need are basic decisions as to where our industry and trade are to head in the years to come. We need some short-term immediate action which will be part and parcel of a long-term plan. We need a minister who will fight like hell for industry.
That is precisely what we now have.

We do not have such a minister now. We need a minister who will pound the table for a capital cost allowance which will compensate for inflation, and who will work with his colleague who is responsible for the finance portfolio for the establishment of an allowance or adjustment which will apply to inventories in place, as present allowances or adjustments do not allow for replacement cost of those inventories.
In short, we need a minister who will bite the bullet, and face the facts of foreign investment legislation in Canada. The fog created by the Foreign Investment Review Board has effectively frightened away investment. The minister is encouraging joint ventures in Canada, but waffling on phase two of the foreign investment legislation. He has failed miserably to put into effect a long-term program to develop a secondary industrial base in Canada. We continue to trade off resources for finished goods.
The minister has made many confusing statements about an industrial strategy, that range from his view that he does not think it possible to develop an industrial strategy in Canada to his statement that he may have 18 or 19 different sectoral strategies. I hope the coming months will show us a little bit about what these strategies are.
The minister is urging Canadian businessmen to go outside Canada, open joint ventures in developing countries, and export back into Canada. His colleague, the Minister of Finance, upon returning from the Middle East, announced recently that Canadians should seek out joint ventures in the Middle East countries.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce when cornered always falls back on that old chestnut that Canadian businessmen are not venturesome, that they are not innovative, and that they are not willing to go out and seek business. Well, let me say that people in industry are sick to death of hearing that story.
The plain truth is that we have a minister who, as the press noted recently, is barely keepling afloat. He is a very average minister, or should I say a barely average minister, a nice guy who likes to philosophize and pontificate about industry and trade, and who loves to use a lot of commercial buzz words.
He is the sort of front-of-the-bus, middle-of-the-road, back-of-the-church fellow who lives in the hope that some miracle will rescue him from his dilemma.
Hear, hear!

Let us take a look at a few industries that clearly illustrate what I am talking about. The automotive parts industry has had a trade deficit with the United States for ten consecutive years. Last year the deficit was in excess of $2 billion. The minister says this is because the U.S. auto industry is down. Well, it certainly

May 28, 1975
Business of Supply
has not been down for the last ten years. The minister has done next to nothing since assuming his portfolio to change this picture.
For years the Americans have endeavoured to make the auto pact a true bilateral agreement. The pact is bilateral from their side and multilateral from our side. As a result of failing to come to grips with this problem, over one and a half billion dollars has been invested in an automotive industry in Brazil, with another billion slated for that country by 1977. Mexico, Argentina, and Venezuela are all building automotive industries. In fact by 1980, automotive production in Brazil will outstrip ours in units produced. We are importing more and more automotive components into Canada from other than North American sources. We are becoming a pass-through assembly operation, and that is tragic. The North American automotive market is being diluted more each year, and our automotive parts industry is dying on the vine.
Take a look at the rubber industry. The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge made some remarks and asked some questions about that. I heard the minister's answers. I was not particularly impressed by them. This industry employs 18,000 people. More than 2,000 have been laid off with little chance of being rehired. We see this industry, which serves a market that consumes 20 million tires a year, being strangled by on-again-off-again tariff policies, and by imported tires. In the past three years we have imported 33 per cent, then 45 per cent, and in 1974, over 60 per cent of the tires we consumed. I will back off on the 60 per cent to this point. We know there were a couple of disastrous strikes in that year, but the fact is that the trend is there. We are importing more and more of the tires we consume in this country.
We only produce half the radial tires required for original equipment production on automobiles and trucks. The tire industry is waiting for some assurance from the minister that he won't give it all away at the GATT meetings in Geneva.
If you were the president of a tire manufacturing company and wanted to get the approval of your board of directors to expand your plant capacity or increase production, what chance do you think you would have if they have a gut feeling that the government is going to pull the rug out from under them at the GATT negotiations? How long can this industry wait for something positive from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce? We know that this industry employs 18,000 people and produces a sales volume of half a billion dollars. We know that they are producing under capacity today and that they can expand their capacity. We know that they have the labour skills, and we know that the market is there.
We also know that we have government in power that does not want to come to grips with inflation or inflationary expectations. We know we have a government in power that is directly responsible for the labour unrest in this country; a government that is overstocked with unimaginative, do-nothing ministers who refuse to face reality. What does the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce propose to do? He suggests we form joint ventures in third world developing countries so we can produce in a cheaper labour market. What the hell is that
going to do for unemployment in Canada? How the hell is that going to improve Canadian export trade?
Shame!

The hon. member says shame. He should be ashamed of his performance.
What the minister should be doing is pounding the cabinet table for a full revision of our tax laws. He should be demanding action on capital cost allowances to reflect inflation. He should be insisting that we maintain the integrity of our currency. He should be setting forth in clear terms our foreign investment policy, and either state the government's clear position on phase two of that policy, or scrap it.
Joint ventures will not flow into Canada in enough volume to affect our unemployment, trade, exports, or balance of payments unless taxation, regulations regarding foreign investments, and capital cost allowances are re-examined, changed, and communicated in precise language. Without this kind of action we will languish in trade imbalances, continued high unemployment, balance of payments deficits, and our recovery from this current recession will lag behind our trading partners some of whom, I might add, have had the courage to take action. We are at a turning point, and what we do in the balance of 1975 and in 1976 will determine our economic activity for the next several years.
We have in our Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce the greatest expertise and talent of any country in the western world. Our GATT negotiators are the most knowledgeable and expert of the group assembled in Geneva, but what are they negotiating toward? Toward what plan are they negotiating? We have no long-range plan for industry in Canada. We have only short-term, ad hoc, patch-work programs; no real incentives to put our resources and labour skills to work on a long-term basis. This comes as no surprise to anyone who looks beyond the facade of glib answers and ghost-written speeches that tumble from the minister's mouth.
As the press acknowledged recently, the minister is treading water. I hope to God that someone will have enough compassion to toss him a rope before he goes under and drags the industry of Canada down with him.
Let us take a brief look at a few of our industries that are in varying degrees of trouble. Many of them are covered by programs. This is why I ask why they are not working. There is the rubber industry, textile industry, automotive production industry, automotive parts industry, feedstock for our chemical industry, the electronics industry, television production, shipbuilding which cannot operate without massive government subsidies, furniture, and footwear. I could list another half dozen or more. This is a pretty sad picture.
When I was in Europe recently I talked to some of the trade people there. The department some months ago sponsored a show for the furniture people in Europe. What do you think they brought over? Canadian designed Scandinavian furniture, chromeplated garbage. Those people are not interested in that. They wanted to see some really good Canadian wood furniture, but they did not get to see that. Somebody along the line muffed on that one.

May 28, 1975

All these industries are in trouble because the government lacks the basic guts to deal with the problems facing industry. The government refuses to deal with inflation, yet is hot on bilingual labelling. It puts in place foreign investment guidelines in clouded terms, then urges Canadians to seek out joint ventures. It has allowed our currency to float, which is inflationary, and has done nothing to improve the integrity of that currency. It pays out billions of dollars in unemployment benefits but has no meaningful retraining program and no industrial strategy through which retrained labour could be channelled.
There is a need for capital investment in Canada, but the government urges Canadian businessmen to form joint ventures in developing third world countries. It is obvious the government is adrift in an uncertain sea with no maps, no rudder and, worst of all, no captain.
