speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak today about a few matters which are now creating new economic and political situations and on which I would like to draw the attention of hon. members because, for my part, I believe that these matters are extremely important, particularly now when we are trying, by all available means, to fight inflation, unemployment and recession and are attempting to find the most stable economic balance possible.
My first subject concerns Canadian industries and foreign capital. To protect Canadian industry, the government has asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) mainly to control the investments of foreign capital in Canada to prevent this economic sector from being invaded by foreign interests and thus to prevent an uncontrolled take-over of our industries by foreigners. This position of our domestic policy is normal and commendable. Certainly, no one here will dispute the value of this policy.
Business of Supply
However, we must realize that this type of decision also has certain drawbacks and often places certain industries which would need mixed capital to survive in serious situations. Unfortunately, Canadian capital is not sufficient to develop adequately our industries. Consequently, businessmen are tempted to seek foreign capital. But now, they cannot do so.
I can quote the recent example of a businessman in my constituency who was just refused such a privilege. Yet, had he been allowed to associate with English interests, his business would have developed to such a point that he could soon have doubled his staff. On the other hand, the government is doing nothing to stop Canadian industries from closing their plants in Canada and from moving to other countries where administration and production costs give them a greater margin of profits. Recently, two Vic-toriaville textile manufacturers announced that they would soon leave Canada for another country.
What is going to happen therefore, Mr. Chairman, if on the one part we prevent industries from developing with foreign capital and on the other part, we allow industries to leave this country? Unless we take rapidly the necessary steps, we shall inevitably witness the slow and last agony of our Canadian industry, which nobody here desires I am sure.
That is why I say: Let us promptly take care of this situation. Shall we broaden our regulations concerning foreign investment? Are we going to resort to incentives to persuade our businessmen to stay here and especially in Quebec? That problem should be dealt with in committees and suggestions from individuals, officials and groups should be studied so as to bring about a quick and efficient solution.
Mr. Chairman, the second question I should like to raise deals with the Industrial Development Bank. This bank, created about 30 years ago, has been of great assistance to the Canadian industry, there is no doubt about that. It was established to encourage Canada's economic prosperity by increasing the efficiency of monetary action through provisions of credit availability for industrial undertakings, by completing the activities on the part of other lenders and by providing help to the small enterprises encountering financing problems.
It is not my intention here to criticize the Industrial Development Bank as to what it was and what it was not, because I prefer dealing with its future. The possibility of making it a Crown corporation is being considered. As for me, I would like to suggest something else. It would seem logical to me and probably more efficient to link it to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and I will give explanations.
Up to now, the part played by the Industrial Development Bank, by reason of its working, was economic. It had to lend money, guarantee loans, acquire shares and put them back into circulation. And because it paid out of its revenue the interest on its bonds, its staff emoluments and all its administration costs, its financial constraints surely obliged it to show wisdom, looked upon as exaggerated by some people, at any rate to temper its spirit of enterprise and avoid risks as far as possible.

May 28, 1975
Business of Supply
I personally know something about this for having helped on various occasions some of my fellow citizens who were trying to get its cooperation. The bank is quite willing to lend to expand a business, for example, but the borrower must prove that he cannot obtain funds elsewhere, that there is already enough capital in the business, and that others like it have invested or are about to invest in it.
I must naturally be convinced of the viability of the business because it bases the amount it may lend on the profit outlook. It is also quite willing to lend to straighten out a financial situation, but it must not be due to incompetence or mismanagement.
Mr. Chairman, it will easily be understood that all those requirements and limitations have affected the efficiency that this financial instrument could have had and they also led to help industries located in the richest provinces, especially those which needed it less, because the risk was smaller. That is why in 1974 the number of loans reached 34 per cent in Ontario, 33 per cent in British Columbia and 19 per cent only in Quebec, and 14 per cent in the Atlantic region. In other words, the provinces where industrial development leaves much to be desired were forgotten. If that development corporation were attached to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, it could be given a political as well as an economic dimension; like the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which gives more grants to underprivileged areas it could thus both benefit and have underprivileged areas benefit from it.
Furthermore, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce already has all sorts of mechanisms to help industry. So the different sectors could combine their efforts. For example, an owner faced with financial difficulties because of a lack of competence in management could first avail himself of the management program, that is the CASE program, which has the advantage of making available at minimum cost a service provided by retired businessmen selected for their experience in management. The owner could thus become eligible for loans from the bank.
Mr. Chairman, surely it will have been noted that my views and my suggestions were directed mainly to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), and that is not by mere coincidence. Having served as Parliamentary Secretary to that department, I was able to fully appreciate its outstanding organization, the competence of those civil servants, the understanding and the communication among departments. I am therefore quite convinced that through that department we could answer both questions I raised today.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I challenge some of the statements of the opposition member who spoke before me. He said that the government and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce lacked imagination and ability; that is how far they went. But I shall ask that and other opposition members what they have to offer.
I listened to every speech this afternoon. We are about to complete consideration of the estimates of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and we heard nothing but criticism from opposition members. Mr. 
Chairman, I also had some criticism about the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, but I did dig into the problem, I studied it to make efficient and positive suggestions. They have no program, no alternative. They say ministers cling to power but, Mr. Chairman, do they believe that they will come into office without any program or any alternative, and just tell Canadians: Now, we shall take the place of the Liberal party. We are Progressive Conservative members and we have no program. We do not have anything to say, we just utter criticism.
I ask the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) especially, since he was the first critic of his party, to listen to me. I was extremely patient in listening to him moments ago, but he actually did not play the role which the opposition should play in this House.
What is aimed at, in this House, is playing partisan politics to have Canadians believe everything is wrong in Canada. Repeating this does no good, because the press gallery is much more receptive to criticisms, as is evidenced by the press reports we read at night before going to bed. We have trouble going to sleep because we read only bad news about Canada, nothing ever would go right.
In effect there are lots of good news. No reference was made to Statistics Canada's last figures on our balance of payments. According to the last figures, our balance is in a surplus position this year. There was no mention of that. Not a word. I submit to hon. members on the other side that although I can criticize within the Liberal party, I am also capable of introducing efficient solutions. If the opposition were to fulfill its true role, it should tell the people: "There is such and such a program. Make use of it, even if it is not perfect. If we gain power, we will change it in such and such a way." This is what the opposition should do, but it does not.
I believe, not as a government member but as a member of parliament, that every hon. gentleman here should double up as information officer to the Canadian public. We have programs. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) announced recently the new shipbuilding industrial assistance program. This program became permanent,-you said earlier we have nothing but temporary measures-the STAP, after an experimental stage, is now the SAP. It became a permanent assistance program to the Canadian shipbuilding industry. Small manufacturers, who are most in need of assistance, are not told about the program that can help small enterprises, as in Quebec for instance, to obtain the expertise they need to rationalize their management, to rationalize their marketing, so that these industries become viable. That is what it is to be a member of this House, period, not a member of the opposition or a member on the government side. That is what I reproach particularly the members of the Progressive Conservative Party with. I believe that the real role of the opposition must be one of cooperation. I readily admit that we should criticize, but it should not be the only thing we do. I have been in this House for many years, almost 13 years, Mr. Chairman, in many occasions I have had the opportunity . .. The member over there who shouts behind the curtain, Mr. Chairman, probably regrets having failed to make suggestions earlier when he was speaking!
May 28, 1975

The Assistant Deputy-Chairman: I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him has expired.

Madam Chairman, in the short time allocated to me it is impossible to give anything more than some small facts about selected areas of our over-all trade problem. Everyone knows that Canada is now faced with the highest imbalance of payments in its history, or at least within the last 25 years, both in actual dollars and real dollars. The obvious reason that the budget has been delayed until June 23, when the government side is so anxious to get out and get home, is that it does not know how to deal with the present combination of rising costs, inflation, and high unemployment.
Furthermore, the Department of Finance is obviously having difficulty forecasting the way in which events will unfold during the summer months. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce seem to be taking refuge in the hope that there will be an upturn in the economy, and particularly in the world economy. But most business forecasts from the United States are bleak. For example it is said that from the business statistics through early May it is not possible to forecast an early upturn in the economy.
The Japanese government is considering changing its two-year policy of tight money "in view of an acute slump in industrial activity in recent months". The West German government is expecting a delayed economic recovery as a result of the world trade recession. It seems probable that the government will stand aside and let the market system operate. This is an expensive answer in terms of unemployment, lost production, and a squeeze on profit.
Much of our troubles, which are certain to get worse before they get better, can be traced to the government's action, or I should say lack of action, in the export field. Our troubles can largely be traced to the government's reaction to our greatest trading partner, the United States.
The history of our trade with the United States is a long and involved one, but I think to some extent the present situation between our two countries can be likened considerably to the trade wars that developed in the thirties. It brings sharply into focus the exchange of views between Mr. Porter, the Unites State Ambassador, and our Secretary of State for External Affairs. Mr. Porter maintains that whatever the relationship between our two countries, it would have to be something special in this world. In other words, because of our close proximity we must have an unusual relationship. But the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that there is no special relationship, and he is also quoted as saying that special relationships no longer serve either of our best interests.
I now wish to talk about this special relationship in the matter of trade and energy. The government told us it was going to conserve oil, first by raising its price to the Americans and thus discouraging them from buying it, and then by phasing out exports to the United States altogether.
Earlier this month the government reversed itself and cut the price of light and heavy crude oil exports by 80
Business of Supply
cents a barrel in order to make Canadian oil more competitive and, incidentally, improve our balance of payments situation. It is obvious that the government is contradicting itself because it has not acted to develop a comprehensive new policy in trade and energy. It is not going to be too long before we reap the whirlwind, and it is going to lead to more unemployment and more inflation.
The decision of the Canadian government to introduce the two-price oil system in 1973 has become more and more a problem. The addition of the export tax of $5 a barrel to the Americans, and the use of this money to finance a subsidy to eastern consumers to offset imported oil at $11 a barrel, has resulted in Canadian oil becoming the highest cost source of oil imports to the United States.
When the government served notice last November that it would phase out exports from a million barrels a day to 650,000 by July, 1975, and to none in 1984, the Americans began looking elsewhere for supplies. Even oil seems to be capable of being priced out of the market. For April, instead of the 800,000 barrels a day authorized, only 600,000 were exported. Canadians thus became a net importer of oil as eastern Canada is importing at a rate of 820,000 barrels a day. Canada is not now making enough on the oil export tax to cover the subsidy to eastern consumers so dependent on imported oil.
Canada has a capacity to produce two million barrels of oil a day with the possibility of exporting approximately one million barrels, but because Ottawa has been so single-minded about curtailing exports to the United States the industry has been forced to shut in 400,000 barrels a day. Investment money is locked in, earning no returns, and thus reducing money available for exploration and development.
This is one area in which the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce must exert itself, and decide what it is going to do about exports in order to earn badly needed foreign exchange. This is the only country in the world to show a decrease in 1974, with a further decrease forecast for 1975. The fact that Ottawa has cut the price of export crude is the first indication that the government is slightly aware of the mess it has spawned. We are losing exports, income and jobs very quickly.
We need a real conservation policy within the country, and this is where the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should be active. We have to consider an increase in the price of domestic oil whether we like it or not, because this will give conservation a real thrust. We must once more consider our industry and our economy in terms of the rest of the world so far as energy prices are concerned. There should be some tax relief for the oil industry so it will have more money and incentive for exploration and development.
Having regard to its balance of payments difficulties, the President of the United States has ordered another $1 tax per barrel on imported oil, and Mr. Ford's energy program is based on the rather practical and simple theory that higher costs will reduce consumption and price control on domestic oil will encourage more production.
This price increase is aimed directly at Canada, designed to shut out our exports as well as those of other exporting nations. Surely the United States would agree to

May 28, 1975
Business of Supply
a supply of oil at a maximum amount per year well into the future. We should aim for this. This should not be so high as to endanger Canadian production. Indeed, it makes sense to export to the United States if we continue to import offshore oil.
The abrupt cessation of oil exports is one of the major causes of our dollar weakness versus the U.S. dollar. The government miscalculated when it felt that the amount of U.S. dollars available for capital inflow did not occur because of the overloading of the U.S. bond market.
In order to facilitate an over-all trading climate with the United States, government policy should be directed toward maintaining the Canadian dollar at close parity with the U.S. dollar. The strong trading linkages between Canada and the United States are what lie behind the two currencies being close to parity. When the economic performances of the two countries differ, as they do now, the danger of a fairly severe exchange rate fluctuation arises. The U.S. economy may not be performing as well at the moment, but it is bringing inflation more quickly under control.
The threat of wage-price inflation is a particularly severe one in respect of our trade imbalance. Devaluation, although supporting trade, could ultimately provide continued support for unrealistic rates of wage, salary and price growth. If devaluation were combined with an attempt at wage and price controls, the outlook would be very serious. Canada will need to attract large*amounts of capital for our huge energy needs in respect of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. Therefore, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should decide whether it wants to proclaim the second part of the Foreign Investment Review Board measure or forget about it, as has been suggested.
Furthermore, a reasonable accommodation with the United States should reduce the influence which the application by El Paso Gas to transport natural gas from Prudhoe Bay to the continental U.S. A. instead of using the Mackenzie Valley pipeline will have. In this way that influence will be blunted. At the present time the main argument of El Paso is that the Canadian administration cannot be trusted. I suggest it is most important that a decision be made in respect of this matter. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has not grappled with this problem of exports, and the problem in respect of exports of oil to the U.S. is most serious, and one of the most important ways, properly handled, to improve our balance of payments position, and in the long run provide a more acceptable solution.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Under the rules of this debate, Madam Chairman, it is going to be very difficult for me to respond to all the points that have been made this afternoon. I will do my best to cover at least some of them.
In the opening statement of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings he referred to R and D, and productivity, and seemed to imply that my department was not interested in sponsoring research and development, or productivity. I would remind him that the program for the Advancement of Industrial Technology, PAIT, and IRDIA are both fundamental to the support of research and development in Canada. I would remind him that the Program for
Industrial Design Assistance is directed toward another aspect of innovation, that is to say, better designs which will sell in Canada and better designs which will sell abroad. I would refer to Fashion Canada, which is a specific program aimed at the clothing and textile industry.
There are other programs which have research and development content. The Program for Defence Industry Productivity has a very important research and development element. Under that program a very significant and new technology has been developed in Canada. I am referring to the D.T.6 and the jet version of that engine produced at U.A.C.L., which has given Canada world leadership in this particular family of motors. I would also refer to the 50-passenger Dash-7, the prototype STOL aircraft which has every promise of being a world leader in its particular category.
I should like to refer the hon. member to a number of other programs because the suggestion was made by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth that we were not interested in producing new programs, and that our programs were all old. I should like to remind him that this is indeed far from the fact. He should be referred to the new changes in the GAAP program, the General Adjustment and Assistance Program, aimed at widening benefits for Canadian manufacturers and those in the service industries who service those manufacturers.
I would like to draw to his attention the new program for the footwear and tanning industry that was introduced about a year ago, and CASE, the counselling assistance for small enterprises that was introduced about a year ago in the House. After a period of development more than 1,000 field workers are now operating across the country and in every province.
I would remind the hon. member that the old shipbuilding program has been replaced with a new program tailored to new needs. The shipbuilding industrial assistance program is aimed at ensuring that that industry will be internationally competitive. It has a built-in incentive for modernization. There are many other programs aimed at assisting Canadian industry to increase its productivity. I referred to several of these in reply to a question by the Social Credit member in respect of the textile industry. There are programs with respect to productivity improvement in the pharmaceutical industry where there is a development assistance program. I have already referred to the Defence Productivity Program and the Industrial Design Assistance Program.
A question was raised by the hon. member for the Social Credit Party concerning what we were doing to ensure that this constellation of programs which are there for the assistance of private industry is made known to private industry. I should like to state that we have intensified our efforts in many ways. For example, we have opened regional offices of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in all provinces across the country.
This government has created the Federal Business Development Bank, which bank will be in business within a very short period of time. I have indicated in the House previously that this bank is more than just a financing

May 28, 1975

institution, which is what the industrial development bank still is. It is an institution which will provide consulting services, management consulting services, to the owner-managers, and which will take over the owner-manager training programs previously undertaken by the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and the technical services which are made available to small businesses by N.R.C. It will provide information services through some 60 different branches across the country. That seems to me to be a constructive way to tell the story and make available to the small businessman the information he can use to make his particular business more competitive or more productive.
I believe it is also important to deal with some of the other questions concerning trade. I could give a long catalogue of the activities this department has initiated over the past year. They are very substantial in terms of outgoing and incoming missions. Something close to 100 incoming and outgoing missions will have been completed in the year 1974-75. In addition there were 51 international trade fairs, exhibitions and seminars abroad in which the department participated and made available to small and larger businesses across the country.
The program for export marketing development has assisted over 3,600 companies since its inception. The payoff on that program has been remarkable. The cost-benefit ratio for this program is indeed in the order of 40 to one. As a result of this program there have been new sales which otherwise would not have taken place in the order of close to a quarter of a billion dollars, at a modest cost to the Canadian taxpayers of $6 million. As I say, the ratio is 40 to one.
We have had more intense activity than ever before in terms of ministerial missions to the newly developing countries and to the potential industrial market for Canada. I am referring to Brazil, Mexico, Cuba, Venezuela, the Middle East countries, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Lebanon and Iraq. We have had missions between Canada and the EEC and between the EEC and Canada. We have had missions to Japan. The role of my department has never been greater than in the past year. In saying all this I think it is important to realize that the government cannot deliver or close a sale with regard to an export opportunity.
It is the responsibility of the government under our system to make available to the private sectors the opportunity to close a sale. We can provide the incentives and the opportunities, but we cannot close a sale. To take the line of the NDP spokesman it would seem to me he would find the solution to industrial problems in Canada by a nationalization. That is not our approach. We think the private sector in the last analysis is the sector that will have to deliver. We are prepared to support those who have shown self-help and those who are the self-starters.
There have been references to some of the industries that are in difficulty at the present time. We are concerned about those industries and are anxious to help them. I have already referred to the action in respect of the rubber and tire industry, and what we are doing in relation to the textile industry in respect of both management and labour as well as the Canadian Textile Institute. I have referred
Business of Supply
to the action we have already taken in respect of imports which are distorting the Canadian market at this time.
I should like to make the point that our approach has been to deal with specific industrial problems on an industry by industry basis rather than as a broadsweeping generalization which really would not get to the heart of the problem. That is the reason why the industrial strategies approach is important. It zeros in on specific industries for specific purposes.
The auto industry is in difficulty today. It would be in much greater difficulty had it not been for the strategy applied in respect of that industry in the mid-1960's. I refer, of course, to the auto pact. Since the auto pact was signed the percentage of Canadians working in the auto industry in North America has increased each year. Investment has increased in Canada over levels that would not otherwise have taken place had it not been for that auto pact. The price differential has narrowed. The auto industry is in difficulty, but by taking an industry approach I think we have served Canada well because we have a more internationally competitive industry which, even though it is hurting, is not hurting as much as its competitors south of the border at the present time.
We have taken the same approach with respect to the shipbuilding industry-I have referred to that already. We have taken the same approach with respect to the footwear industry, and we are presently working with the furniture industry in trying to provide for them a rationalization assistance, clearly providing the over-all perspective, the over-all climate, saying to them, "What are you prepared to do?" because in our system it seems to me that the companies themselves have to take action; we cannot legislate what each particular company will do. We can provide the incentives and the assistance, as we have done and will continue to do.
I think I am close to the end of the time allotted to me, but I would like to reiterate what I said at the beginning, that we are emphasizing research, development, and productivity, we are emphasizing export opportunities, and what we ask of the Canadian private sector is that they seize these opportunities and make use of them. We cannot do it for them, but we sure as hell will help them.

Madam Chairman, I was most interested in the comments of the hon. member for Halton-Went-worth-I see him behind the curtain-who suggested that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce should be ashamed of himself because he has frightened away foreign investment with, as he said, the fog of the Foreign Investment Review Act. I also believe the minister should be ashamed of himself, but that is not the reason, in my view, for which he should be ashamed of himself. He should be ashamed of sitting here and presiding over the continuing takeover of Canada by foreign corporations, and of failing to introduce to the House meaningful foreign investment review legislation which would stop the continuing erosion of Canadian sovereignty caused by the takeover by foreign investment. What has been going on in this country is nothing short of a scandal. The minister must take the responsibility for it because it is his department that is supposed to be administering that legislation.

May 28, 1975
Business of Supply

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Tell the B.C. government to sell their products in Canada instead of selling them in the United States.

I would be perfectly happy to say that to all the provincial governments in this country, all of which have copped out on the major issue of protecting Canadian sovereignty. I am much more interested in listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Windsor West who makes the same point over and over again, and who wishes the minister could come forward with what his report really meant, and give to Canada the kind of leadership that many other countries in the world have embarked upon a long time ago.
According to the latest count we have about 90 takeover bids, 80 of which have been approved. Let us look at some of these. In this country 99 per cent of the petroleum industry is foreign owned. One of the recent approvals is for Pacific Petroleum Limited of B.C., controlled by Pacific Petroleum of the United States, to take over Wizard Oil Limited of Montreal. This legislation sets forth ten separate criteria. The last of those criteria-that is one out of ten-is that the takeover be compatible with the industrial and economic policy. How in heaven's name is the Foreign Investment Review Agency to justify the taking over of the last tiny percentage of Canadian ownership in the oil industry on the basis of significant benefit for Canada?
That is why I say this legislation has become a farce, a laughing stock among those many people in the country who are finally waking up to the fact that Canadians are independent and that we have a sovereignty to protect. We have to stop selling ourselves out for every buck that comes across the border. One of the reasons why we have high real estate prices in British Columbia is that 67 per cent of the new investment has not been domestic but has come in from Hong Kong. It has driven our cost of land up to a tremendous degree.
I do not want to run through the litany of foreign ownership. Making an investment in this country right now is as hard as joining the Book of the Month Club or passing a skill testing question after you have joined a supermarket contest. There is no real review mechanism at all, otherwise we would not have these ridiculous takeovers being continually approved.
I want to ask the minister several questions before I sit down because I think they are significant in terms of where we go in administering the present legislation. First, what are the reasons for the decisions that are given by the Foreign Investment Review Agency which are published, and can those reasons for the decisions be appealed, or does the public have access to them?
The second question is one regarding good corporate citizenship, one of the criteria that the Foreign Investment Review Agency uses. I refer specifically to the Reed Group paper company takeover of the Alpha Group when the Reed Group has continually been polluting the Grassy Narrows Indian Reserve with mercury, yet this does not seem to affect the decisions that are made. I do not know whether there is interdepartmental consultation about the corporate citizenship of those who are applying for approval of takeovers.

Third, how many corporations have received the advice that they are deemed to be Canadian corporations without having to go through the review mechanism? Also, how many have received advice on how to get around the provisions by the simple expedient of changing their stock or reducing their capitalization below the reviewable amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
On the first question which the hon. member asked regarding the reasons about the decisions not being published, I should like to make two points. First of all, we are providing information on how the particular transaction meets the criteria in the act. Each time I announce the cabinet's decision with respect to allowances and disallowances, we publish a schedule which shows all the companies for which an allowance was given. I think there are something like 90 different colums, and we indicate how that particular transaction met the particular criterion. If it meets it, there is an indication.
Also, we have been trying to provide more information on some of the major transactions so that the public can understand what the benefits were that were negotiated in rather more specific terms. For example, in the Reed-Alpha transaction which the hon. member mentioned there was a considerable amount of information given. I am speaking from memory but, as I recall, the transaction will result in close to 2,700 new jobs in northwestern Ontario. That is because as a result of that transaction and what it involved, which was a vertical integration on the part of a purchaser of a distributing organization, he was prepared to go ahead and make a major investment in Northern Ontario. There is interdepartmental consultation, of course, with respect to this transaction.
To answer the last question of how many companies have been given binding rulings with respect to their eligibility or non-eligibility, I do not have the number at my fingertips but I think it is something like 20, and I can check that. I can assure the hon. member that there has not been the kind of jiggery pokery he implied in his question. We are interested in real control, not the cosmetics, the point being that if a company has, for example, a 15 per cent foreign share ownership we will look at that very closely, although it is a long way from 51 per cent, because it is possible in certain circumstances that 15 per cent could be controlling. If it were, of course, that company would be found to be a non-eligible person.
The second point in that connection is that these rulings are subject to two things-they are firm for two years only, and of course binding only if there is no material change in the circumstances of the particular corporation.

Madam Chairman, I should like to point out to the minister with regard to the Reed Alpha group takeover that Reed Alpha had been fined previously approximately $25,000 under the Combines Investigation Act, as I understand it. disincentives which chase industry to other parts of the world.
